slides.content: – Given: numeric outputs for each test example (e.g. 𝑃(𝑦= 1|𝑥)) – Approach 1. Sort output values for test set 2. Locate boundaries between examples with different labels 3. Compute the FPR and TPR for each of these boundaries 4. Plot each (FPR,TPR) point 5. Connect the points to construct the curve Constructing a ROC curve 34

slides.title: Convex hull of a ROC curve
slides.content: Convex hull of a ROC curve TPR FPR 0.0 1.0 1.0 – Each point in the ROC space is a classifier – Best classifier depends on operating conditions – Costs – Class skew – Convex hull: Set of best classifiers under some operating condition – Classifiers that are not on the hull → Never optimal under the considered linear cost settings. – How do we get all the classifiers on the hull? → Interpolation 44

slides.title: – ROC can be misleading if:
slides.content: – ROC can be misleading if: #positive examples << # negative examples – ROC looks at fractions, not total numbers – If lots and lots of negative examples, then a very low FPR can still mean lots of FPs – E.g., Cancer diagnosis, search results, anomalies – Solution: Precision and Recall ROC: class skew 48

slides.title: – Partition examples into k disjoint sets
slides.content: – Partition examples into k disjoint sets – Create k training sets – Each set is union of all folds except one – So each set has 𝑘−1 𝑘 of the original training data Solution 2: Cross validation 80

slides.title: – Smaller data → More folds
slides.content: – Smaller data → More folds – If you have very little data (<100 examples), you can use leave-one-out cross validation – Set number of folds to the number of examples – For n examples, train your classifier n times on n-1 examples – Involves no random subsampling, every instance is used n-1 times as training data and once as test data – Typically, people use 5-fold or 10-fold cross validation – With large datasets (>1 million examples), a single split into train-test is OK! Cross validation in practice 82

slides.title: – Representativeness problem:
slides.content: – Representativeness problem: – All examples from a whole (infrequent) class might be missing in the training data – Error estimate is then meaningless One potential problem 83

slides.title: – Representativeness problem:
slides.content: – Representativeness problem: – All examples from a whole (infrequent) class might be missing in the training data – Error estimate is then meaningless – Solution: Stratification – Ensure that each class is represented with its original class proportion in both train and test sets – Error estimates bear meaning – Variance in estimates will reduce One potential problem 84

slides.title: – Possible that held aside test data is not representative of new data gathered
slides.content: – Possible that held aside test data is not representative of new data gathered as test data! – Even with correct methodology: – Positive and negative examples collected differently – Features acquired differently for different classes – The split should mimic deployment and keep dependent observations together! – Examples: – Cancer samples processed by different people or on different days than normal samples – Song belongs to a playlist on one day, not on the other Big Pitfall: is test data representative of real data? 85

slides.title: – Data is stratified before the cross validation is performed
slides.content: – Data is stratified before the cross validation is performed – All data is used for testing! – The predictions over the test folds are concatenated or the error estimates are averaged to yield an overall error estimate – Because we use multiple training sets in Cross-Validation, we are evaluating a learning method as opposed to an individual learned model – Did I tweak my algorithm a million times until I get good results? – Solution: Use one or two datasets for development, then expand evaluation Notes on cross-validation 86

slides.title: – This can be for a variety of reasons:
slides.content: – This can be for a variety of reasons: – Tools may support only real-valued features or only discrete features – Can improve computational efficiency – String comparisons are slower than integer comparisons – Fewer options to try = faster run time – Can improve accuracy – Two categories of operations – Manipulating the values a feature can take on – Removing features Manipulating the feature space 88

slides.title: – Convert ordinal to numeric which enables using > or <
slides.content: – Convert ordinal to numeric which enables using > or < – E.g. Tempo={Very slow, slow, quite slow, normal, quite fast, fast, very fast} →Very slow=1; slow=2; quite slow=3; normal=4, … – One-hot encoding of nominal features – One binary indicator per value Transforming ordinals and nominals Genre Jazz Punk Opera Genre=Jazz Genre=Punk Genre=Opera 1 0 0 0 1 0 0 0 1 Note: converting to integers incorrectly implies there’s an ordering or relation between categories when there isn’t 89

slides.title: – Group values into categories by hand
slides.content: – Group values into categories by hand – Map e.g. US states to regions; subgenres into genres; years into decades – If many infrequent values, group them (e.g., new category “other”) – Target encoding: Replace each feature value with a statistic derived from the target – Real: e.g. Average of target for each value – Discrete: e.g. Conditional probability of target for each value Handling features with many possible values Artist Plays Skipped Target Encoding ABBA 100.000 20.000 0.20 Green Day 50.000 20.000 0.40 Eminem 75.000 25.000 0.33 Skrillex 33.000 27.000 0.81 90

slides.title: – Feature selection: Remove features prior to learning
slides.content: – Feature selection: Remove features prior to learning – Why? – Easier learning: Fewer parameters (good if |Features| ≫|Data|) – More interpretable models: Gain domain insights – Improve efficiency: Fewer features = less memory / runtime – Better performance: Irrelevant attributes degrade performance – How? – Filter-based approaches – Wrapper-based approaches Feature selection 93

slides.title: – Idea: Measure each feature’s usefulness in isolation (i.e., independent of other
slides.content: – Idea: Measure each feature’s usefulness in isolation (i.e., independent of other features) – Pro: Scales to large feature sets or large data sets – Cons: – Misses feature interactions – May select redundant features Filter-based feature selection All features Feature selection Algorithm: assign a score to each feature Pick top k features 94

slides.title: – Metric that computes a “correlation”
slides.content: – Metric that computes a “correlation” – Information gain with S the data and A the feature: – Pearson correlation coefficient with fi the ith feature and y the target: – Single-variable classifier: Select based on predictive performance – Build classifier with just one variable – Discrete: Decision stump – Continuous: Threshold the feature’s value – Measure performance Two filter-based approaches 95

slides.title: – Feature selection = search
slides.content: – Feature selection = search – State = set of features – Start state – Forward: No features – Backward: All features – Operators: – Forward: Add a feature – Backward: Remove a feature – Scoring function: Model’s performance when using the state’s feature set Wrapper-Based feature selection 96

slides.title: – Forward
slides.content: – Forward – Faster in early steps because fewer features to test – Fast for choosing a small subset of the features – Misses features whose usefulness requires other features (feature synergy) – Backward – Fast for choosing all but a small subset of the features – Preserves features whose usefulness requires other features (e.g., area requires both length & width) Forward vs backward 99

slides.content: – Problem: Often have to tune multiple parameters: – E.g. Random forests: number of trees, depth of trees, width of trees, … – Approach: Treat as a search problem – Grid search: Try all possible values – Random search: Sample possible values – is often quite effective (why?) → Random search works well because usually only a few hyperparameters strongly affect performance, so it tests more distinct values of those parameters than a grid with the same budget. slides.title: – Need a reasonable spread of values:
slides.content: – Need a reasonable spread of values: – Good: t = 50, 100, 500, 1000 – Bad: t = 40, 45, 50, 55, 60 – Good: k = 1, 5, 15, 25 – Bad: k = 1, 3, 5 – Good: λ = 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5, … – Bad : λ = 0.01, 0.02, 0.03 – Reasoning: Spread between values is important – Idea: Use log-spaced values for scale parameters and choose bounds based on plausible values and computational budget. Values to be considered 110

slides.title: – Information from outside the training set leaks into the training data (i.e., test
slides.content: – Information from outside the training set leaks into the training data (i.e., test set is no longer independent) – Happens more often than you think – Common errors: – Global preprocessing, e.g., feature selection or target encoding before cross validation. Must repeat entire data processing pipeline on every fold of CV using only that fold’s TRAINING DATA – Temporal dependencies: Use future data to predict the past – Incorrect or misaligned time stamps – Multiple examples for each entity: Must do cross validation on the subject level and not the example level Leakage 111
